title: Hobbies & Free Time
subtitle: Talk about what you love doing when you are not working

lessons.title: Mes loisirs
lessons.description: Name your hobbies and learn the difference between "jouer à" and "jouer de".

blocks.heading: Talking about your free time
blocks.body: Hobbies are "les loisirs" in French. To say what you enjoy, start with "j'aime" (I like) or "j'adore" (I love). To say what you actually do, use "je fais" (I do) or "je joue" (I play).

examples.french: Pendant mon temps libre, je lis.
examples.english: In my free time, I read.

examples.french: Mon loisir préféré, c'est le dessin.
Je fais de la danse le mardi.
Nous jouons aux échecs le soir.
examples.english: We play chess in the evening.

blocks.tip: "Loisir" is usually plural: « Quels sont tes loisirs ? » — What are your hobbies?

blocks.heading: Asking someone about their hobbies
blocks.body: Two questions will take you a long way: "Quels sont tes loisirs ?" and "Qu'est-ce que tu fais pendant ton temps libre ?". Answer with "moi, je..." to make it personal, and add "préféré" (favourite) to talk about the one you love most.

examples.french: Qu'est-ce que tu fais pendant ton temps libre ?
examples.english: What do you do in your free time?

examples.french: J'ai un nouveau loisir : la photo.
examples.english: I have a new hobby: photography.

blocks.tip: In French, a colon and a question mark both take a space before them: « un nouveau loisir : la photo » and « Ça te plaît ? ».

blocks.heading: jouer à or jouer de?
blocks.body: Use "jouer à" for games and sports, and "jouer de" for musical instruments. Don't forget the contractions: à + le = au, à + les = aux, de + le = du.
blocks.tip: Quick memory trick: a game is something you play AT (à), an instrument is something you make music OUT OF (de).

blocks.heading: faire de + activity
blocks.body: For many activities — sport, dance, drawing, music in general — French says "faire de". The same contractions apply: de + le = du, de + les = des.

examples.french: Je fais du sport trois fois par semaine.
examples.english: I do sport three times a week.

examples.french: Il fait de la photo le dimanche.
Je ne fais pas de sport.
examples.note: after a negative, du/de la become simply "de"

blocks.tip: "Faire" is irregular: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font.

lessons.title: Le sport
lessons.description: Name the sports you practise and say what you like, prefer and hate doing.

blocks.heading: Which sport do you do?
blocks.body: The question is "Tu fais du sport ?" — do you do any sport? Answer with "je fais de..." for most activities, or "je joue à..." for team and ball sports. Both patterns are extremely common, so learn them side by side.

examples.french: Oui, je fais de la natation.
Je joue au football le samedi.
Elle fait du vélo tous les matins.
Nous faisons de la randonnée en montagne.
examples.english: We go hiking in the mountains.

examples.french: Mon père ne fait pas de sport.
examples.english: My father doesn't do any sport.

blocks.tip: Ball sports played with a team usually take "jouer à": le football, le tennis, le basket, le volley.

blocks.heading: Where and how often
blocks.body: Add a place with "à la piscine", "au stade", "au parc", and a frequency with "une fois par semaine" (once a week) or "tous les jours" (every day).

examples.french: Elle joue au tennis avec sa sœur.

blocks.tip: "Une fois" = once, "deux fois" = twice, "trois fois" = three times. Add "par semaine" or "par mois".

blocks.heading: aimer / préférer / détester + infinitive
blocks.body: To say what you like doing, put the second verb straight after in the infinitive — no extra word in between. This works with aimer (to like), adorer (to love), préférer (to prefer) and détester (to hate).

examples.english: I prefer running in the morning.

examples.french: Nous n'aimons pas regarder le football.
Tu préfères jouer au tennis ou au basket ?
examples.english: Do you prefer playing tennis or basketball?

blocks.tip: English uses "-ing" (I like swimming), French uses the plain infinitive (J'aime nager). Never say « J'aime nageant ».

blocks.heading: The verb préférer
blocks.body: "Préférer" changes its accent depending on the ending: é becomes è when the ending is silent. Listen for the difference — préfère sounds open, préférons sounds closed.
blocks.tip: Same pattern as "répéter" (to repeat): je répète, nous répétons.

lessons.title: Le week-end
lessons.description: Say what you do at the weekend, use "on" like a native, and invite a friend out.

blocks.heading: What do you do at the weekend?
blocks.body: "Le week-end" covers Saturday and Sunday. Use "le samedi" and "le dimanche" with "le" to mean "every Saturday / every Sunday", and drop the "le" for one particular day.

examples.french: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
examples.english: What are you doing this weekend?

examples.french: Le samedi, je fais les courses.
examples.english: On Saturdays, I do the shopping.
On Saturday, I'm going to the cinema.

examples.french: Ce week-end, il y a une fête chez Léa.
examples.english: This weekend, there is a party at Léa's.

blocks.tip: "Bon week-end !" is what everyone says on Friday evening — answer "Merci, toi aussi !".

blocks.heading: Inviting a friend
blocks.body: French invitations are short and friendly. "On va au cinéma ?" already means "Shall we go to the cinema?". You can also use "Tu veux..." (do you want to) or "Ça te dit de..." (do you fancy).

examples.french: On va au parc cet après-midi ?
examples.english: Shall we go to the park this afternoon?
Do you want to come with us?

examples.french: Ça te dit d'aller au musée ?
examples.english: Do you fancy going to the museum?

examples.french: Désolé, je ne peux pas samedi.

blocks.tip: To refuse without sounding rude, always give a small reason: « Désolé, je ne peux pas, je travaille. »

blocks.heading: "On" means "we"
blocks.body: In everyday French, "on" replaces "nous" almost all the time. The important part: "on" takes the same verb form as "il" and "elle" — always the third person singular.

examples.english: Shall we play tennis on Saturday?

blocks.tip: Say "on" in conversation and "nous" in writing — that is exactly what French speakers do.

blocks.heading: Inviting, accepting, refusing
blocks.body: An invitation can simply be "on" + verb with a rising voice. To accept, use "avec plaisir", "bonne idée" or "d'accord". To refuse, start with "désolé" and give a reason.

examples.english: Do you want to go to the park?

examples.french: Désolée, je ne peux pas, je travaille.

blocks.tip: A woman writes "désolée" with two e's; a man writes "désolé". The sound is exactly the same.

passages.title: Une invitation
passages.french:
— Salut Nora ! Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
— Samedi, je travaille. Mais dimanche, je suis libre.
— Super ! On fait une randonnée dimanche matin, ça te dit ?
— Bonne idée ! On part à quelle heure ?
— À neuf heures, devant le parc.
— D'accord, à dimanche !

— Hi Nora! What are you doing this weekend?
— On Saturday, I'm working. But on Sunday, I'm free.
— Great! We're going hiking on Sunday morning, do you fancy it?
— Good idea! What time are we leaving?
— At nine o'clock, in front of the park.
— Okay, see you on Sunday!
